claim: DFW's Terminal F modular program placed six mega-modules using self-propelled modular transporters, the largest 278 ft by 136 ft and weighing 3,320 tons, publicly described as the largest modules ever moved for a terminal expansion.
source_title: DFW Terminal F Modular Construction: Precision and Partnership
supporting_excerpt: fabricating six mega-modules offsite, then moving them down a taxiway and setting them in place in August 2025. The largest module measured 278 feet by 136 feet and weighed 3,320 tons, a record-setting feat that DFW and the JV describe as the largest modules moved for a terminal expansion at any airport.
airport_or_entity: DFW / Innovation Next+ JV (Archer Western, Turner, Phillips May, H.J. Russell)
caveat: Description originates from the JV's own communications; module dimensions are physical facts but the 'largest at any airport' framing is a claim by the parties.

claim: The Terminal F first phase is scheduled to open with 15 gates in 2027 and modular methods accelerate the project timeline by as much as 30 percent.
source_title: Dallas Fort Worth Airport completes record-breaking modular move as new Terminal F construction reaches major milestone
supporting_excerpt: The first phase, now underway, is due to open with 15 gates in 2027. Much of the terminal is being built in modular sections that can be moved into place, accelerating the project timeline by as much as 30 percent.
caveat: The 30% number is a sponsor/consultant estimate and not an independently audited figure.

claim: DFW and American announced acceleration and expansion of Terminal F to 31 gates at approximately $4 billion, with the Use and Lease Agreement extended through 2043.
source_title: DFW Airport and American Airlines Announce Acceleration and Expansion of Plans for Terminal F
supporting_excerpt: 31 gates ... approximately $4 billion ... Use and Lease Agreement extended through 2043.
caveat: Program cost is a rounded planning figure at time of announcement.

claim: FAA AC 150/5300-13B, Airport Design (2022, Change 1 with errata), sets the geometric design standards for runways, taxiways, aprons, and other airfield facilities including standards keyed to Aircraft Design Group.
source_title: AC 150/5300-13B, Airport Design, Change 1 with errata
page_or_section: chapters 1-6 (Introduction, Design Principles, Runway Design, Taxiway and Taxilane Design, Aprons, Airfield Systems and Facilities)
supporting_excerpt: The AC contains chapters on: (1) Introduction, (2) Design Principles, (3) Runway Design, (4) Taxiway and Taxilane Design, (5) Aprons, and (6) Airfield Systems and Facilities.
caveat: AC guidance not creating new rulemaking but is the design standard federally funded projects must meet.

claim: FAA Advisory Circular 150/5360-13A, Airport Terminal Planning (2018), is the current federal terminal planning framework and does not create new requirements.
source_title: AC 150/5360-13A, Airport Terminal Planning
supporting_excerpt: This AC does not create new requirements for airport terminal planning.
caveat: AC is guidance; sponsors adopt as design basis.

claim: FAA AC 150/5380-7B includes an appendix on Pavement Management Program requirements and an appendix on the Pavement Condition Index method for airfield pavements.
source_title: AC 150/5380-7B, Airport Pavement Management
page_or_section: Appendix A (PMP) and Appendix B (PCI Method)
supporting_excerpt: added a new Appendix A on Pavement Management Program (PMP) requirements and Appendix B on the Pavement Condition Index (PCI) Method.
caveat: Referenced across FAA pavement guidance stack.

claim: FAA AC 150/5320-17A provides the visual rating framework for airfield pavement condition (Pavement Surface Evaluation and Rating manuals) used when a full PCI survey is not feasible.
source_title: AC 150/5320-17A, Airfield Pavement Surface Evaluation and Rating Manuals
supporting_excerpt: The FAA recommends the information and procedures contained in the manuals for use by airport staff and consultants when it is not possible to complete a more detailed pavement condition index (PCI) survey as part of a more comprehensive pavement maintenance management program.
caveat: PASER-style visual rating; supplements but does not replace full PCI.

claim: CBP's Airport Technical Design Standard sets a benchmark of approximately 100 passengers per hour per double primary booth and a minimum primary queue depth of 50 to 75 feet at U.S. international airports with FIS operations.
source_title: PARAS 0052: Planning Considerations for International Arrivals Facilities
page_or_section: CBP throughput and queue standards section
supporting_excerpt: One hundred passengers per hour per double booth is the CBP standard for passenger processing. Additionally, the minimum queue depth at any U.S. airport with international service is required to be at least 50 feet (75 feet normally).
airport_or_entity: U.S. Customs and Border Protection / applicable to all FIS airports
caveat: CBP ATDS is republished on a roughly three-year cadence; 2021 edition is the version PARAS 0052 references.

claim: The CBP Airport Technical Design Standard is republished on a roughly three-year cadence, with the 2021 edition currently governing FIS design.
source_title: PARAS 0052: Planning Considerations for International Arrivals Facilities
supporting_excerpt: FIS facilities at US international airports are currently governed by the Airport Technical Design Standard (ATDS), version 2021. The ATDS is published every three years by CBP and provides an elaborate set of design guidelines and standards for commercial airports.

claim: ACRP Research Report 252 assumes a 15-year replacement cycle for baggage handling machinery, with annual EDS maintenance costs of approximately 10 percent of purchase cost per unit.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 252: Airport Baggage Handling System Decision-Making Based on Total Cost of Ownership
supporting_excerpt: maintenance calculations consider a 15-year replacement cycle, with the second installation of machines occurring after 15 years ... Annual EDS machine maintenance costs are assumed to be approximately 10% of purchase cost per unit.
caveat: Report guidance; actual airport lifecycles vary with utilization.

claim: ACRP Research Report 186 provides guidance for considering life-cycle costs in airport asset procurement.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 186: Guidebook for Considering Life-Cycle Costs in Airport Asset Procurement
supporting_excerpt: Guidebook for Considering Life-Cycle Costs in Airport Asset Procurement
caveat: Framework document; not a per-airport cost dataset.

claim: MARS (Multiple Aircraft Ramp System) stands are engineered to accommodate either one Code E widebody or two Code C narrow-body aircraft, using multiple lead-in lines, dual boarding bridges, and engineered clearances.
source_title: Destination: MARS
supporting_excerpt: A Multiple Aircraft Ramp System (MARS) gate is a flexible gate design that can accommodate either one widebody or two narrowbody aircraft at once. The same stand can be used to serve either two smaller aircraft (Code C or smaller) or one larger aircraft (Code D, E, or F).
airport_or_entity: TYLin / industry application (Helsinki, O'Hare T5, others)
caveat: MARS stand configurations vary; specific dimensions are project-dependent.

claim: At a modular airport project, module placement was validated with laser survey to a placement tolerance of approximately three-quarters of an inch.
source_title: Managing Risk in Modular Construction Using Dimensional and Geometric Tolerance Strategies
page_or_section: case discussion of airport site placement tolerances
supporting_excerpt: At airport sites specifically, connection points were validated with laser survey to support accurate placement with ¾ inch tolerance.
airport_or_entity: unnamed airport case study within modular construction industry
caveat: Not DFW-specific; illustrative of the tolerance regime the method demands.

claim: Denver International Airport terminated the Great Hall P3 concession 14 months after construction began, after the contractor projected roughly $311 million of overrun against a $650 million contract price and up to three years of delay.
source_title: Denver International Airport Will Terminate The Great Hall Renovation Contract
supporting_excerpt: by mid-2019, Great Hall Partners and its builder were projecting a $311 million cost overrun against the $650 million contract price and a delay of as much as three years
caveat: Reporting of contractor projections; final figures evolved further.

claim: Denver airport paid $184 million to end the Great Hall P3 partnership and later approved a completion path with Hensel Phelps totaling approximately $2.1 billion, with completion expected in 2028.
source_title: The Denver Great Hall P3 Terminated After 14 Months...
supporting_excerpt: It cost DIA $184 million to end the partnership ... DIA expects to finish the project with a new firm, Hensel Phelps, in 2028 for a total of $2.1 billion.
caveat: Secondary consulting analysis; totals to be confirmed against final DIA financials.

claim: An independent audit of Denver International Airport's oversight of the Great Hall project found the airport lacked sufficient oversight of large projects.
source_title: After DIA's Great Hall construction issues, the Auditor's Office says airport officials don't have enough oversight of big projects
supporting_excerpt: the Auditor's Office says airport officials don't have enough oversight of big projects

claim: Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) failed to open on its scheduled May 2012 date after failure of the fire protection system, and continued to experience problems with smoke extraction, fresh air supply in the event of fire, and baggage handling systems through subsequent delays.
source_title: Construction of Berlin Brandenburg Airport
supporting_excerpt: It became clear on 8 May 2012 that the building could not open on schedule, officially due to the failure of the fire protection system. The airport had problems with fire safety, smoke extraction system, and fresh air supply in the event of fire.
caveat: Wikipedia summary; primary sources include Bundestag inquiries and FBB filings.

claim: Heathrow Terminal 5 was built under the T5 Agreement, a relational contract in which BAA carried the risk and integrated first-tier suppliers on a cost-plus-fixed-fee basis to enable a single systems-integration discipline.
source_title: Heathrow Terminal 5 - Improving Delivery Models
supporting_excerpt: The T5 agreement was a cost-plus contract with BAA paying the suppliers' actual cost plus an agreed fixed fee covering their overheads and profit, based on a partnering approach.
caveat: Widely cited GIH case; specific contract terms in academic and industry literature.

claim: Bent Flyvbjerg's dataset of over 16,000 projects finds that approximately nine out of ten megaprojects experience cost overruns, with airport-related examples including Denver International's original build at approximately 200% real-cost overrun.
source_title: What You Should Know About Megaprojects, and Why: An Overview
supporting_excerpt: Overruns of up to 50 percent in real terms are common, over 50 percent not uncommon. Cost overrun for the Channel tunnel was 80 percent in real terms. For Denver International Airport, 200 percent.
caveat: Denver figure is for the original 1990s airport, not the Great Hall renovation.

claim: Delta Air Lines and the LGA Airfield Reconfiguration team completed the $2.8 billion LaGuardia Terminal C program early, with the airline fully completing the four-concourse terminal by the end of 2024, nearly two years ahead of the original plan.
source_title: Delta Air Lines Inc. & LGA Airfield Reconfiguration Team Has Early Finish on $2.8B Airport Project
supporting_excerpt: the airline fully completed the entire four-concourse terminal by the end of 2024, almost two years earlier than originally planned
airport_or_entity: Delta Air Lines / Port Authority of NY & NJ / LaGuardia
caveat: Early finish attributed in part to re-sequencing during COVID traffic trough.

claim: Delta's LGA construction team re-sequenced work during the COVID-era traffic trough to accelerate concourse construction, structural steel erection, and curtain wall installation, shaving nearly a year off the schedule.
source_title: First-Class Arrival: New Delta Air Lines Terminal C
supporting_excerpt: The team re-sequenced work to take advantage of the lower airport traffic, which enabled them to accelerate critical phases like concourse construction, structural steel erection and curtain wall installation. Ultimately, the team's COVID strategy helped shave nearly a year off the schedule.
caveat: Vendor case study; consistent with contemporaneous reporting.

claim: American Airlines' new Admirals Club at DFW Terminal C will occupy approximately 37,000 square feet, described as the airline's largest anywhere and larger than the existing DFW Flagship Lounge in Terminal D (~25,000 sf).
